scenario.title: A quote the team can stand behind
scenario.description: A field-service company receives requests through email and PDFs. Estimators reconcile them with ERP records, route exceptions through an approval queue and assemble reports from disconnected sources. I work through a proposed design that makes the evidence, commercial commitment and delivery responsibility visible together.
scenario.boundary: D-01: prepare a source-backed quote draft. A named, authorized person must approve before sending. The pilot prepares drafts and records approval only; sending and dispatch remain in the existing human-operated workflows. It has no autonomous sending or dispatch capability.
scenario.label: Worked design exercise. The organization, inputs, estimates and targets are illustrative. This is not a shipped client engagement or a claim of measured results.

executive.label: Executive sponsor
executive.opening: I am proposing a bounded way to help estimators prepare quotes with clearer evidence and accountability. I am not promising faster turnaround until we measure it.
executive.question: Which delay matters enough to address, and who can authorize the investment?
executive.show: The current handoffs, proposed pilot boundary, effort range, dependencies and evidence required for a continuation decision.
executive.decision: Sponsor discovery and a bounded pilot. Keep approval, sending and dispatch with authorized people.

engineering.label: Engineering team
engineering.opening: The proposed service reads approved sources, prepares a draft and records a human decision. It does not acquire permission to send quotes or dispatch work.
engineering.question: Can we preserve source identity, access boundaries and reproducible calculations across every draft revision?
engineering.show: The data contract, read-only ERP adapter, deterministic pricing calculation, versioned draft and approval state machine.
engineering.decision: Validate the integration and evaluation design before estimating an implementation as ready to build.

risk.label: Risk and assurance
risk.opening: A plausible answer is insufficient. Every material quote detail needs an allowed source, and the software cannot approve its own work.
risk.question: What evidence proves that unauthorized access, stale prices and bypassed approvals fail safely?
risk.show: The threat review, source permissions, retention plan, negative tests, approval record and revocation procedure.
risk.decision: Accept the bounded pilot only after its controls are demonstrated and residual risks have named owners.

operations.label: Operations team
operations.opening: The draft should make an estimator's work easier to check. Missing information enters an owned queue instead of becoming a confident guess.
operations.question: Who handles an incomplete request, a rejected draft or an unavailable source during a busy shift?
operations.show: The exception queue, source links, approval handoff, existing send process, support runbook and fallback workflow.
operations.decision: Agree ownership and rehearse the exception paths before people depend on the pilot.

stages.title: Prepare before the first conversation
stages.lead: I prepare around the decision the business needs, not a product demonstration. I separate what I know from what I need to ask, then make the meeting useful for the people attending.
actions: Research the service model, request channels, current systems and likely business constraints.
Identify the sponsor, estimator, ERP owner, security reviewer and delivery decision makers.
Send a short agenda, evidence request and proposed decision for the session.

artifact.title: Preparation brief
lines: Known scenario: email and PDF intake, ERP records, an approval queue and fragmented reporting.
Hypothesis to test: repeated reconciliation contributes more delay than drafting the response.
Request: approved sample requests, workflow walk-through, access constraints and available timing data.
Meeting outcome: agree the problem, owner and evidence needed before proposing a build.

stages.exit: The meeting has an accountable sponsor, a decision and the right operational voices.
stages.hold: Do not assume a bottleneck or prepare a production promise from public research alone.

stages.title: Know the room and change the explanation
stages.lead: I explain the same proposal differently to each audience. The sponsor needs the investment decision; the estimator needs the changed work; engineering and assurance need the boundaries they must prove.
actions: Confirm who decides, who advises, who operates and who can stop release.
Open with the audience's question, then offer the supporting technical depth.
Ask each group to explain the proposed boundary back in their own words.

artifact.title: One decision, four views
lines: D-01 remains constant: source-backed draft, named approval, human sending and dispatch.
Sponsor: is a bounded pilot worth the effort and operational attention?
Engineering and risk: can the draft be traced, constrained and independently checked?
Operations: who owns the queue when a request cannot proceed?

stages.owner: Engagement architect with the customer sponsor
stages.exit: The groups agree what is being decided and can identify their own responsibility.
stages.hold: Resolve conflicting expectations before an audience-specific explanation becomes a different promise.

stages.title: Observe the work and establish a baseline
stages.lead: I follow a request through the real handoffs before designing a replacement. I need to understand the exceptions, data ownership and existing controls as well as the happy path.
actions: Walk through intake, clarification, pricing, approval, sending and dispatch with their owners.
Map source permissions, freshness, document quality and the authority for price changes.
Agree how to measure preparation time, rework, approval waits and operating cost.

artifact.title: Current-state evidence map
lines: Request PDF → estimator → ERP lookup → approval queue → human send → dispatch team.
Unresolved: which ERP fields are authoritative and whether request timestamps are reliable.
Baseline: not measured. Record preparation time separately from time awaiting customer clarification.
Process-only alternative: improve the intake form and queue ownership before adding AI.

stages.owner: Operations process owner and data owners
stages.exit: The team agrees the workflow, evidence gaps, baseline method and decision to investigate.
stages.hold: No savings claim or automation recommendation without a usable baseline and source ownership.

stages.title: Design the boundary before the assistant
stages.lead: I compare a better process, conventional automation and an assisted draft. The design earns its complexity only if it improves the work while keeping authority, evidence and recovery clear.
actions: Define the Azure foundation, identity boundaries, environment separation and read-only integration.
Plan governed ingestion, OneLake ownership, Fabric workspaces, reporting and capacity assumptions.
Evaluate Copilot Studio and Foundry against channel, integration, ownership and operational requirements.

artifact.title: D-01 architecture decision
lines: Email/PDF intake → controlled extraction → allowed ERP retrieval → draft → named human approval.
Price arithmetic uses validated ERP values and deterministic rules; missing values stop the draft.
Draft evidence includes source, revision and retrieval time. Document instructions are untrusted input.
Software identities cannot send, dispatch or approve. A revised draft requires fresh approval.
Platform choice remains conditional on a validated integration and operational fit.

stages.owner: Design authority with security, data and integration owners
stages.exit: The chosen option has a recorded trade-off, threat review and testable boundary.
stages.hold: Pause if source permissions cannot be preserved or human approval can be bypassed.

stages.title: Turn the design into an honest commitment
stages.lead: I estimate the work as a set of deliverables and dependencies. The technical scope, commercial approval and customer acceptance belong to named roles, with uncertainty visible before anyone commits.
actions: Write the SOW with deliverables, exclusions, role effort, milestones and acceptance evidence.
Validate delivery capacity, licensing, environments and access before promising dates or prices.
Record assumptions and route scope changes through impact assessment and written approval.

artifact.title: Illustrative pilot SOW
lines: Included: one intake route, one read-only ERP adapter, draft review queue, reporting and handover.
Excluded: automatic sending, dispatch, ERP writes, broad data cleanup and additional business units.
Estimate by role and work package, with low and high person-hours, dependencies and contingency shown separately. The interactive planning envelope above carries the current example values.
Dependencies: approved samples, API access, available reviewers, capacity and licensing confirmation. Effort is illustrative, not elapsed duration or a quote.
Change example: adding an ERP write requires revised controls, effort and acceptance before approval.

stages.owner: Technical scope owner, delivery lead and commercial approver
stages.exit: Customer and supplier approve the scope, commercial terms, dependencies and acceptance process.
stages.hold: Do not absorb unapproved scope or turn a planning range into an unconditional deadline.

stages.title: Prove the uncertain part in a rehearsal
stages.lead: I use a bounded rehearsal to test the riskiest assumptions. A convincing demonstration needs a failure path and clear limitations, otherwise it can sell a level of readiness the team has not earned.
actions: Prepare approved or synthetic examples with expected results and source permissions.
Rehearse missing prices, stale records, conflicting documents and embedded malicious instructions.
Let the estimator reject a draft and explain what happens next.

artifact.title: Rehearsal script
lines: Normal case: draft cites allowed request and ERP records; the estimator checks its calculation.
Missing price: hold for clarification, with no invented amount or silent fallback.
Injected instruction: treat PDF text as evidence, never as authority to change permissions.
Proof required: approval cannot be self-issued and no send or dispatch operation exists.

stages.exit: The evidence supports continuing, changing the design or stopping, with limitations recorded.
stages.hold: A passing rehearsal does not establish production reliability, savings or deployment readiness.

stages.title: Keep the build aligned with what was agreed
stages.lead: I keep design authority through delivery while the delivery lead owns planning and execution. We review risks together and make changes visible before they become customer surprises.
actions: Assign work to platform, data, application and quality owners with explicit interfaces.
Review architecture decisions, pull requests, control evidence and deviations on a regular cadence.
Escalate a breached assumption with impact, options, recommendation and the next customer update.

artifact.title: Delivery decision record
lines: Design authority: architecture integrity and exceptions. Delivery lead: plan, resources and dependencies.
ERP delay: describe the blocked work, re-sequencing option and effect on the agreed milestone.
Customer update: what changed, who owns resolution, the decision needed and when we report again.
Every scope change links back to D-01, its estimate and its acceptance evidence.

stages.exit: The implemented scope has review evidence and no hidden exceptions to the agreed boundary.
stages.hold: Stop affected work when an access, safety or scope breach cannot be contained.

stages.title: Make readiness a decision with evidence
stages.lead: I make release readiness explicit. The customer should see what passed, what remains uncertain and who accepts the residual risk, including the practical route back to the existing workflow.
actions: Run authorization, source isolation, approval replay and stale-data tests against the release candidate.
Verify operational monitoring, retention, cost limits and recovery with the responsible owners.
Walk the sponsor through acceptance evidence and the remaining risks before release approval.

artifact.title: Pilot release gate
lines: Required: allowed sources only, reproducible calculations, revision-bound approval and attributable audit events.
Required: failure paths route to an owned queue; sending and dispatch remain outside the pilot.
Fallback: disable new draft creation and return requests to the established estimator workflow.
Decision record: release version, evidence, residual risks, named approvers and recovery owner.

stages.owner: Customer release approver with security and operations owners
stages.exit: Authorized owners accept the evidence and the team has rehearsed the fallback.
stages.hold: An unresolved authorization failure or missing operational owner blocks release.

stages.title: Measure the work after the demonstration
stages.lead: I compare observed work with the agreed baseline. A shorter draft time is not enough if review effort, errors or operating cost increase. The continuation decision should use the whole workflow.
actions: Track preparation time, correction rate, queue age, adoption, availability and cost per reviewed request.
Review source freshness, incident patterns, access changes and capacity with operational owners.
Decide whether to continue, adjust or retire the pilot using recorded evidence.

artifact.title: Outcome review
lines: Baseline and observed results: not measured in this design exercise.
Proposed comparison: similar request types, the same measurement definitions and a declared observation period.
Record preparation and approval waits separately; distinguish assisted requests from requests handled manually.
Keep business outcomes, platform consumption and commercial commitments as separate measures.

stages.owner: Operations owner with the sponsor and service owner
stages.exit: The next investment decision has evidence, limitations and a responsible decision maker.
stages.hold: Do not claim attributable savings from adoption counts, a demonstration or incomplete timing data.

stages.title: Leave a team that can own the system
stages.lead: I build enablement into the engagement from the first workshop. Handover is complete when another person can explain the boundaries and handle an exception, not when I have sent a document.
actions: Pair an architect or operator with preparation, delivery reviews and customer conversations.
Use shadowing, teach-back and a short debrief to turn observation into independent judgment.
Provide runbooks, decision history, access procedures and an owned improvement backlog.

artifact.title: Shadow, explain, operate, teach
lines: Prepare: learner states the audience, decision and risks before the session.
Debrief rubric: accurate explanation, appropriate depth, clear ownership and honest handling of uncertainty.
Operate: learner handles a missing source, rejected draft and fallback using the runbook.
Teach: learner explains why human approval remains necessary and documents the next improvement.

stages.owner: Technical mentor and operations enablement owner
stages.exit: The receiving team demonstrates the operating and communication skills it needs.
stages.hold: Workshop attendance is not proof of competence or a substitute for an accountable service owner.

stages.title: Turn earned evidence into the next opportunity
stages.lead: I make partner collaboration useful to the customer. A joint account plan connects a real need to capable delivery, with customer permission and program eligibility checked before funding or co-sell is presented as available.
actions: Align the customer sponsor, account team and partner on the next decision and responsibilities.
Verify current Microsoft partner, co-sell and funded-engagement requirements for the specific opportunity.
Reuse sanitized architecture and outcome evidence only with the customer's permission.

artifact.title: Joint account and evidence brief
lines: Customer need: a next phase supported by measured pilot evidence, not a predetermined expansion.
Account plan: sponsor, delivery capacity, technical owner, commercial owner and agreed next action.
Program gate: verify eligibility, application, written approval and conditions before assuming support.
Reference gate: customer permission, sanitized material and accurate separation of commitments and realized outcomes.

stages.owner: Customer sponsor, partner account lead and practice lead
stages.exit: The next pursuit has permission, credible evidence, delivery ownership and a clear commercial path.
stages.hold: No guaranteed funding, automatic co-sell entitlement or customer reference without permission.
